```{r}
UniversalBank <- read.csv("C:/Users/sophi/Downloads/UniversalBank (1).csv")
summary(UniversalBank)
library(caret)
library(class)
library(gmodels)

# Selecting the three variables
UniversalBank <- UniversalBank[, c("Online", "CreditCard", "Personal.Loan")]

# Renaming the variables
names(UniversalBank) <- c("Online", "CC", "Loan")

# Converting the variables to factors
UniversalBank$Online <- as.factor(UniversalBank$Online)
UniversalBank$CC <- as.factor(UniversalBank$CC)
UniversalBank$Loan <- as.factor(UniversalBank$Loan)

# Selecting 60% of the data for training
set.seed(123)

train_rows <- createDataPartition(
  UniversalBank$Loan,
  p = 0.6,
  list = FALSE
)

# Creating the training dataset
Train <- UniversalBank[train_rows, ]

# Creating the validation dataset
Validation <- UniversalBank[-train_rows, ]

# Checking the size of each dataset
nrow(Train)
nrow(Validation)


# QUESTION A

# Creating the pivot table
Pivot_A <- table(
  CC = Train$CC,
  Loan = Train$Loan,
  Online = Train$Online
)

# Showing the pivot table
ftable(
  Pivot_A,
  row.vars = c("CC", "Loan"),
  col.vars = "Online"
)



# QUESTION B

# Calculating the probability of loan acceptance
Loan_Probability <- 51 / (51 + 467)

# Showing the probability
Loan_Probability

```
Among the 518 customers who have a credit card and use online banking, 51 accepted the loan. The probability of accepting the loan is 51/518 = 9.85%.

```{r}
# QUESTION C

# Creating the pivot table for Loan and Online
Pivot_Online <- table(
  Loan = Train$Loan,
  Online = Train$Online
)

# Showing the first pivot table
Pivot_Online

# Creating the pivot table for Loan and CC
Pivot_CC <- table(
  Loan = Train$Loan,
  CC = Train$CC
)

# Showing the second pivot table
Pivot_CC


# QUESTION D

# Calculating P(CC = 1 | Loan = 1)
P_CC1_Loan1 <- 84 / 288

# Calculating P(Online = 1 | Loan = 1)
P_Online1_Loan1 <- 176 / 288

# Calculating P(Loan = 1)
P_Loan1 <- 288 / 3000

# Calculating P(CC = 1 | Loan = 0)
P_CC1_Loan0 <- 777 / 2712

# Calculating P(Online = 1 | Loan = 0)
P_Online1_Loan0 <- 1611 / 2712

# Calculating P(Loan = 0)
P_Loan0 <- 2712 / 3000

# Showing the probabilities
P_CC1_Loan1
P_Online1_Loan1
P_Loan1
P_CC1_Loan0
P_Online1_Loan0
P_Loan0

```
Among the customers who accepted the loan, 29.17% have a credit card and 61.11% use online banking. Among those who did not accept the loan, 28.65% have a credit card and 59.40% use online banking. Overall, 9.6% accepted the loan and 90.4% did not.

```{r}
# QUESTION E

# Calculating the probability score for Loan = 1
Loan1_score <- P_CC1_Loan1 * P_Online1_Loan1 * P_Loan1

# Calculating the probability score for Loan = 0
Loan0_score <- P_CC1_Loan0 * P_Online1_Loan0 * P_Loan0

# Calculating the Naive Bayes probability
NB_Probability <- Loan1_score / (Loan1_score + Loan0_score)

# Showing the probability
NB_Probability

```
Using the Naive Bayes formula, the probability that a customer with a credit card who uses online banking will accept the loan is approximately 10.01%.

```{r}
# QUESTION F

```
The pivot table gives a probability of 9.85%, while Naive Bayes gives 10.01%. The pivot table is more accurate for the training data because it uses the actual observed proportions without assuming conditional independence between the predictors.

```{r}
# QUESTION G

library(e1071)

# Training the Naive Bayes model
NB_Model <- naiveBayes(
  Loan ~ CC + Online,
  data = Train
)

# Showing the model output
NB_Model

# Predicting probabilities for the training data
NB_Predictions <- predict(
  NB_Model,
  Train,
  type = "raw"
)

# Selecting a customer with CC = 1 and Online = 1
Matching_row <- which(
  Train$CC == 1 & Train$Online == 1
)[1]

# Showing the probability of Loan = 1
NB_Predictions[Matching_row, "1"]

```
The calculation uses the prior probabilities of Loan = 1 and Loan = 0, and the conditional probabilities of CC = 1 and Online = 1 for both loan classes. The Naive Bayes model gives a probability of 10.01%, which matches the result calculated manually in Question E.
